sections.title: Keystones
sections.intro: Answer these first: they set what a session promises, which calls Natalie makes alone, how long and how far a turn runs, and what the world may do to your PC. Your PC is your player character, an NPC is anyone else, OOC (out of character) is table talk outside the fiction, a Front is a threat with a clock, and the Ledger is the running bill of costs.

questions.title: What a session promises
questions.question: Whatever the thread, what does every session at the table promise you?
questions.context: No rule says what a session owes. R57-10 forbids rigging either way; R70-114 keeps one warm bond per thread. Apocalypse World's game master plays "to find out what happens" (Baker); web serials pay off a beat every chapter; Blades in the Dark shows the city has moved between jobs.

options.label: Play to find out
options.consequence: Natalie preps situations, never plots: NPCs with wants, Fronts with clocks, places with trouble. No outcome is settled before you act, and no session is steered back to a planned beat.

options.label: A payoff and a bill
options.consequence: Every session puts at least one earnable payoff in reach (a read that lands, a debt collected, a re-assay, the Guild's fresh measure of a practitioner) and leaves one cost on the Ledger. Nothing is handed over unearned.

options.label: The world moved
options.consequence: Every session shows you at least one thing that changed without your PC: a price, a death, a notice posted, a door shut. The world keeps its own hours.

options.label: A warm beat
options.consequence: Every session gives the thread's warm bond a moment of its own (a meal, a joke, a hand on a shoulder), on top of R70-114's thread-level duty.

questions.rec_reason: Together they are the table you describe: fair because nothing is decided in advance, LitRPG-satisfying because a payoff is always reachable, grimdark because the bill and the moving world never stop. R70-114 already keeps the warmth at thread level.

questions.title: Improvise or ask
questions.question: At the table, which calls does Natalie make herself, and which wait for you?
questions.context: R48-26: invent NPCs, places and texture "without asking, logged; bigger things wait for Isaac." "Bigger" is never defined, and CLAUDE.md's "Nothing waits on Isaac" and your "make the calls" pull the other way. About sixty "pending Isaac" flags sit in the notes of fifty-nine table scenes, several of them stalling play.

options.label: Natalie decides everything
options.consequence: "Bigger things wait" is struck. Natalie makes every call, even a carded NPC's death or a new faction, and logs each as an agent ruling (a call you may overturn) at the turn's foot.

options.label: Only your own wait
options.consequence: Natalie makes and logs every call except facts about your own characters (their past, kin, body, Stage), which she asks in one OOC line at the turn's foot while play carries on.

options.label: Canon changes wait
options.consequence: Anything that would change a card, a canon page or a rule waits for your word, and the turn writes around it until you answer.

options.label: As written
options.consequence: R48-26 unchanged: Natalie judges case by case what counts as bigger.

questions.rec_reason: It ends the pending pile you asked to end and keeps back only what is truly yours, your characters' lives; numbers never wait either, since R70-99 prints an unsourced figure as a marked estimate.

questions.title: How long a reply runs
questions.question: What length does each kind of reply run at?
questions.context: R48-28 and R49-30 make every reply a full turn of about 3,500 words, "even to a quick line or question." NATALIE.md still prints the old bands (300 to 700 for talk), and Discord turns run a median 1,506 words. Open: whether an OOC (out of character) question, a ruling or a correction counts as a reply.

options.label: 3,500, every reply
options.consequence: R49-30 as written: any reply, OOC ones included, comes as a full turn of about 3,500 words.

options.label: 3,500 in fiction only
options.consequence: Every in-fiction turn runs about 3,500 words, even to one quick line; an OOC question, a ruling or a correction gets a plain answer at its own length, with no prose attached.

options.label: Bands by scene type
options.consequence: This reopens R49-30: talk and interior turns run 2,000 to 3,000 words, standard turns 3,500, set pieces 5,000 and up (R48-46). Fights keep R71-5's pace.

options.label: Sized to your post
options.consequence: This reopens R49-30: a one-line post gets about 1,500 words, a full beat 3,500, a set-piece prompt 5,000 and up.

questions.rec_reason: It keeps your own answer ("3500") for every turn of fiction, and a rules question stops coming back wrapped in a scene you did not ask for.

questions.title: How much story a turn covers
questions.question: How much story time does one turn cover before it stops?
questions.context: R49-29 fills a turn half with texture and talk, half with the world moving; R48-29 lets dull stretches pass in a line. In practice one exchange took one turn: the Geturo bout ran eight files. Jo-ha-kyū (the Noh tempo: slow start, building middle, swift close, R70-15) shapes set pieces only.

options.label: One moment, deep
options.consequence: A turn renders one beat of story, a few minutes at most, slow and lush. The richest prose and the slowest play.

options.label: Run to the next choice
options.consequence: A turn covers as much story as passes before your next real decision: the walk, the wait, the talk around it. Routine is skipped and pressure slowed, so talk runs by the line and travel by the hour.

options.label: Fixed by scene type
options.consequence: Talk and fights run one beat a turn; travel, searches and downtime run a day a turn, stopping early only at a threat.

questions.rec_reason: A 3,500-word turn should carry story instead of padding one exchange; B lets the clock speed up and slow down on its own, the way the web serials you name keep pace.

questions.title: Standing orders outside fights
questions.question: May you post standing orders in talk, travel and investigation, as R71-5 lets you in a fight?
questions.context: A standing order is a move declared in advance. R71-5: you post conditions ("if he closes, I cut low") and Natalie runs them "until the first branch they do not cover." Elsewhere Table Rule 1 stops every turn at your next decision, so a search or an interrogation moves one choice per turn.

options.label: Fights only
options.consequence: R71-5 stays a combat rule; in every other scene the turn stops at your next decision.

options.label: Every scene type
options.consequence: Post conditions anywhere ("if she names the stair, I ask for the daybook"). Natalie runs them to the first branch they miss, and any line your PC speaks is only your posted words.

options.label: Routines only
options.consequence: Travel, watches, searches and downtime take standing routines that run to the first surprise; talk still stops at each line that presses your PC.

questions.rec_reason: It is the contract you already trust in a fight, it speeds up the slow investigation turns, and Natalie still never chooses or voices anything you did not write.

questions.title: What the world may do to your PC
questions.question: Outside a fight, what may a turn write on your PC without your hand?
questions.context: R49-01 lets narration go "to full depth" inside your PC, you overruling; R71-6 makes his wounds world facts and leaves the read to you, but only in fights. Open: his involuntary reactions (sweat and nausea from Pressure, the weight a higher Stage puts on a room, R70-69; a flinch at a shot) and what he would know that you might not.

options.label: Reflexes as world facts
options.consequence: Involuntary responses (sweat and nausea under Pressure, a startle, cold shakes, a drug taking hold) land on his body as facts, as wounds do under R71-6; what he does next stays yours.

options.label: Evidence, never the conclusion
options.consequence: In talk and investigation too, Natalie lays the tells in the room and never draws his conclusion; the deduction is your post, R71-6's "the read his" carried outside fights.

options.label: What he would know
options.consequence: What your PC knows and you might not (a custom, a Guild form, the feel of a Stage) comes as plain recall, from his card and canon only, never a new memory.

options.label: Feelings stay posted
options.consequence: This narrows R49-01: narration names no emotion, wish or decision you have not posted, and its depth reaches only sense, body and carded memory.

questions.rec_reason: They keep the world honest on his body and his knowledge fair, while the choice and the deduction stay yours; D would undo the interior depth R49-01 gave you on 2026-09-26.

questions.title: The world that moves unseen
questions.question: When the world moves out of your PC's sight, how much of it does a turn show you?
questions.context: NATALIE.md holds "ninety percent of the world under the surface"; R49-09 lets a turn close on "a short, clearly marked cut" to what the POV (the point-of-view character) cannot see. Anime cuts to the villains' meeting; the iceberg keeps it dark. Every sample: Harrowgate sends a sealed note about the Finding of Cause off the grounds.

options.label: Only what he meets
options.consequence: No cutaways at the table; off-screen moves reach the page only as evidence your PC runs into. R49-09 stays for written scenes.
options.sample: A Visitation runner takes the east-range stair two steps at a time and goes past the dispensary door without slowing, a satchel strap worn pale across his chest. The flap is buckled over a single folded sheet. At its edge shows a corner of green wax, still glossy, the seal pressed so lately that the impression has not dulled. Below, the lodge door bangs behind him, and the hum in the stone takes the sound and keeps it.

options.label: A cutaway, reasons kept
options.consequence: One marked cutaway a session, at a turn's close, when a Front moves: it shows the act and keeps the reason, as R70-76 does for the world's magic.
options.sample: *The Visitation Room.* Harrowgate writes three lines, sands them, and tips the sand back into its box without losing a grain. She folds the sheet twice. The wax goes on green, and she presses the seal with the burned hand, holding it down a breath longer than the wax needs. The runner waits at the door with his cap in both fists. She gives him the note and one word, "Wire," and turns back to the empty line on the Finding.

options.label: A cutaway, all shown
options.consequence: Cutaways may close any turn and show the act and the reason, so you as author see the world's machinery while your PC knows only what he meets.
options.sample: *The Visitation Room.* Harrowgate writes to the Grand Mage's office in three lines. If the Academy's inquiry instructor will not sign, she will draw the Finding herself before her circuit report goes up, and the party answerable will be whichever Class X student costs the charter least. She sands the page, seals it in green with the burned hand, and gives it to the runner with one word, "Wire." Then she dips her pen.

questions.rec_reason: It keeps the anime cutaway you licensed in R49-09 and still leaves nine tenths under the water, so your PC's read stays the game.

sections.title: The turn
sections.intro: How one turn is built, from its first line to the notes under it, plus the session's openers: the "previously" line, the Rumor Mill (world news at session start, some of it wrong) and the Scene Menu (three hooks when you arrive without a beat). The prose samples are roleplay turns in the present tense (R49-02), set in the Aetherion Academy thread, and your PC Rovhen only ever does what the context says you posted.

questions.title: Opening a turn
questions.question: How does a turn open on what your PC just did?
questions.context: Table Rule 1 says "answer what the PC did" and never says whether the turn first writes that action out again. AI roleplayers call the habit parroting: spending the opening on what the player already wrote. Every sample answers your post: Rovhen turns the Finding face down and says, "Open the book, Examiner."

options.label: Open on the answer
options.consequence: The first line is the world's response, and your action is never restated, since you wrote it. Leanest; a reader of the archive needs your post beside the turn.
options.sample: Harrowgate's palm stays flat on the ledger. Her eyes go once to the overturned form, where the ink dot shows through the back of the paper as a grey shadow, and come up again. "The inspector's book belongs to the circuit," she says. "It opens before witnesses, at the quarterly, for the man who carries the gauge." Through the closed casement Sallow's hammer starts on the next plate of row six, and the note comes back dull. She does not turn her head toward it.

options.label: Your move, in full
options.consequence: The turn first renders your posted action and line in full prose with the room around them, then the world answers. The archive reads like a novel, and a quarter of the turn goes to your move.
options.sample: Rovhen takes the Finding by one corner and turns it over on the leather, and the blank beside *Party answerable* goes face down with the ink dot inside it, a grey shadow through the back of the paper. The hum runs on in the floorboards. "Open the book, Examiner." Harrowgate's palm stays flat on the ledger. "The inspector's book belongs to the circuit," she says. "It opens before witnesses, at the quarterly, for the man who carries the gauge."

options.label: One clause, then answer
options.consequence: Your move gets one clause that fixes where it landed, then the world answers. The archive stays readable and the turn spends itself on what you did not write.
options.sample: With the Finding face down between them and his question still in the room, Harrowgate keeps her palm flat on the ledger. Her eyes go once to the grey shadow of ink through the back of the paper. "The inspector's book belongs to the circuit," she says. "It opens before witnesses, at the quarterly, for the man who carries the gauge." Outside, Sallow's hammer finds the next plate of row six, and the note comes back dull.

questions.rec_reason: It cures parroting without leaving the archived turn unreadable, and nearly all of the 3,500 words go to what you could not have written yourself.

questions.title: Where a talk turn stops
questions.question: In a talk scene, how far does a turn run before it stops for you?
questions.context: Table Rule 1: stop at his next decision, on an NPC line, an action or a thing he can see, never on an OOC question; R70-17 lets a turn stop mid-crisis. A talk scene offers a chance to speak every few lines. Every sample answers your post asking for the inspector's book and shows its turn's last lines.

options.label: First opening
options.consequence: The turn stops at the first moment your PC could speak or act. Shortest stretch of story and the most control; the 3,500 words go to the room around that moment.
options.sample: Harrowgate's palm stays on the ledger while Sallow's hammer works along row six outside the casement. She looks at the overturned form, then at him, with the same clean attention she gave the page she sanded. "The book opens for the circuit, Rovhen. Before witnesses, at the quarterly." She lifts the grounding tea, finds the cup empty, and sets it back on its ring without a sound.

options.label: First pressure
options.consequence: The turn runs past pauses he would let pass and stops when something presses him: a question to him, an offer, a threat, a clock. A line aimed at him always stops it.
options.sample: Harrowgate tells him the book opens for the circuit, and her words are still in the room when boots come up the stair, one knee favoured. Sallow sets a cased plate on the corner of the desk, square on the Finding, and raps the brass back with a fingernail. It gives a dull note. "Row six, Examiner. Rang like a wet boot, the lot." He turns his creased face to Rovhen. "You're Lambert's lad. Lambert would've had that book open by now. Will you?"

options.label: The scene's hinge
options.consequence: The turn runs to the scene's turning point (the reveal, the demand, the deadline), carrying the NPCs' talk among themselves past several openings. Nothing addressed to him is passed over.
options.sample: Sallow comes up the stair favouring one knee, sets the cased plate on the Finding, tells the Examiner the row rings like a wet boot and the bill is hers, and goes down favouring the other. Harrowgate draws the form out from under the brass by one corner. The frame scrapes a pale line across the leather. She turns the blank toward Rovhen and lays the pen across it. Across the quad the first bell begins to count, and the bead at the nib lets go onto *Party answerable*.

questions.rec_reason: Your PC stays answerable to everything said to him while the room gets to breathe, and every stop lands on a thing he must meet, which is Table Rule 1's intent.

questions.title: Several NPCs in one turn
questions.question: When several NPCs share the room, how does a turn carry their talk?
questions.context: R48-43 allows one crafted speech, and R70-111 lets court cultures, the Accord chancery among them, argue at length. The Cabin turns carried thirty-seven to forty-two lines of speech each, nearly all from one NPC. Every sample: Harrowgate and Sallow in the Visitation Room after you ask for the book.

options.label: One voice leads
options.consequence: One NPC carries the turn's talk; the others get a gesture or a single line. Clear and quiet, and the second NPC's want waits its turn.
options.sample: Harrowgate answers him and nobody else. "The book is the circuit's, Rovhen, and the circuit sits at the quarterly." Behind her Sallow sets the cased plate on the corner of the desk, folds his scorched arms, and says to the window, "Rings like a wet boot." Harrowgate goes on as if the plate were a teacup. "The Finding wants a hand. Yours would settle it in a morning, before witnesses, with your class there to watch it done."

options.label: The room talks
options.consequence: NPCs talk to each other, interrupt and score points, and your PC overhears what they would never tell him; the turn stops when the room turns to him.
options.sample: Sallow gets in first. "Book won't tell him what the plate will." He drops it on the Finding, brass up. "Quarter punch struck twice and off true." "Master Sallow, the bursar pays wardwork." "Bursar says you've got the chain, so you've got the bill." "You have opinions about everything you are paid for." "I'll say them till I'm paid." Harrowgate's burned hand closes over the other by a knuckle's width, and both of them turn in the same breath to Rovhen.

options.label: Each turns to him
options.consequence: Each NPC addresses your PC in turn with what it wants. Every want arrives at once, and the stop carries several asks.
options.sample: Harrowgate speaks first, and to him. "The book stays shut. The Finding wants a hand, and yours would settle it." Sallow waits her out, sets the plate on the desk and speaks to him too. "You're Lambert's lad. You'll want the punch on that brass before you sign anything." From the landing, where she will not cross the threshold, Agnes Tull calls in, "Wire's come down for you, Instructor. Nine words, and your name spelt wrong again."

questions.rec_reason: Exposition through disagreement is the house way of keeping the iceberg, Dickens is a named model, and the Sallow and Harrowgate scene, your best-kept thread, already works like this.

questions.title: Routine talk in summary
questions.question: May a turn tell routine talk in summary and quote only the lines that matter?
questions.context: The law wants realistic dialogue (R48-43) and voices nobody could swap, and never says every word must be quoted. Novelists move between scene (every line given) and summary (talk reported in a sentence). Every sample: Sallow and the bursar's clerk haggle over row six at the lodge window while Rovhen waits for his key.

options.label: Every line quoted
options.consequence: All speech in a turn is direct and quoted. Full texture, and routine haggling eats a share of the 3,500 words.
options.sample: "Row six entire, son. Six plates." "The Academy pays per plate cracked, Master Sallow." "None of them's cracked. They're cased." "Then the Academy pays for none." "Then the Academy can stand under that dome when the next Class X match lets go." The clerk wets his pen. "The charter says per plate." "Charter never stood under a dome." Sallow leans in at the window. "Six plates rang dull, and somebody signed them sound. You want that on your bursar's book, or the Visitation's?"

options.label: Summary, then the line
options.consequence: Routine exchange (prices, directions, greetings, haggling) is told in a sentence or two; any line that carries a want, a lie, a refusal or a tell is quoted in full.
options.sample: Sallow and the bursar's clerk go three rounds over row six at the lodge window, the clerk quoting the charter and Sallow quoting the clerk back to himself, until the clerk runs out of charter and reaches for the pen-wipe instead. Then Sallow leans in at the window. "Six plates rang dull, son, and somebody signed them sound. You want that on your bursar's book, or on the Visitation's?"

options.label: Mostly reported
options.consequence: Speech is mostly reported, and only the last line is quoted. Lean and fast, and the voices blur together.
options.sample: At the lodge window Sallow and the bursar's clerk argue over row six. The clerk says the Academy pays per plate cracked; Sallow says none of them are cracked, they are cased, and the bill is for the row. The clerk cites the charter, and Sallow says the charter never stood under the dome. In the end he leans in at the window and asks one thing. "Bursar's book, or the Visitation's?"

questions.rec_reason: It spends the turn's words where the game is, on wants, lies and tells, and it matches how the novelists you name pace a scene.

questions.title: When the world interrupts
questions.question: When your post chains several actions or a long speech, where may the world cut in?
questions.context: Table Rule 1 forbids resolving "a multi-decision action in one go", and R19-2 keeps your PC's words unaltered. Neither says whether an NPC may cut him off mid-line, or where a chain of actions ("I pick the lock, slip in, read the ledger") stops.

options.label: Your post lands whole
options.consequence: Everything you post happens as written, and the world answers after. Simple, and a chained post can slide past a guard who would have stopped it.

options.label: Actions cut, speech whole
options.consequence: A chain of actions stops at the first point the world pushes back, and the later actions never happen; every line he speaks is said in full, though NPCs may react while he speaks.

options.label: Both may be cut
options.consequence: As B, and an NPC may also talk over him at a sentence break; the unsaid rest returns to you, and the turn stops on the interruption.

questions.rec_reason: NPCs who would refuse do refuse (Table Rule 3), and your words stay yours to the last syllable, as R19-2 wants.

questions.title: Table talk and notes
questions.question: Where do OOC talk and the author notes sit at the Desktop table?
questions.context: R48-47: full author notes "go in the scene file" and "chat gets a short summary." Claude Desktop keeps no scene file per turn, so the notes either ride in chat or wait for the archive, and R48-50's one-line pushback needs a place too. A Discord post Natalie drafts for you carries none of it.

options.label: Foot now, file at archive
options.consequence: Prose first; below a rule, a short foot of OOC lines. The full notes are written once, when archive_scene (the tool that files a finished scene) saves it.

options.label: Head now, file at archive
options.consequence: One OOC line before the prose and nothing after it; the full notes are written at archive.

options.label: Full notes every turn
options.consequence: The foot plus the full notes (rule ids, Stat Ledger of running figures, research) in chat under every turn. Nothing waits for the archive, and every turn grows long.

options.label: A separate reply
options.consequence: The turn is prose alone; OOC lines and notes arrive as a second short message.

questions.rec_reason: The fiction ends on its stop with nothing between you and the decision, and the notes still get written in full once, where R48-47 wants them.

questions.title: What the foot carries
questions.question: What goes in the short OOC foot under a turn?
questions.context: The full notes carry rule ids, the Stat Ledger, research and costs (R48-47, R14-3). The foot is what you actually read every turn. You use rule ids to correct the index, and an agent ruling is a call Natalie made that you may overturn.

options.label: Calls made
options.consequence: One line per call Natalie made this turn (a new NPC, a fact, an estimate), each marked as an agent ruling you may overturn.

options.label: What it cost
options.consequence: The Ledger lines and Front ticks the turn caused, one line each, so nothing is lost before the session close.

options.label: Rules and the deciding row
options.consequence: Two to four rule ids that bound the turn and, for any adjudicated outcome, the stat row that decided it (R14-3).

options.label: A state line
options.consequence: One status line, a LitRPG status bar: place, hour, your PC's wounds and reserve as world facts, and what is owed next.

questions.rec_reason: A and B are what the session close keeps losing, and C is how you correct the index; D repeats what the prose and the Stat Ledger already hold.

questions.title: The "previously" line
questions.question: How does a session's first turn put you back in the scene?
questions.context: Sessions sit days apart, the State of Play pages (one where-we-are page per thread) run weeks stale, and the Kharven thread straddles two moments a year apart. The archive's scene files open on an italic place-and-hour line; AI roleplay tools pin a memory note. Every sample opens the fifth day of term at first bell, the Finding due.

options.label: Place and hour
options.consequence: An italic header (place, day, hour), as the scene files open; the prose re-grounds everything else.
options.sample:
*Aetherion Academy, the old dispensary. The fifth day of term. First bell.*

The bell is still counting over the east range when the Visitation runner reaches the dispensary door. Rain has darkened the shoulders of his coat. He stands with one hand out, palm up, the way a toll-keeper waits for copper, and his eyes go past Rovhen to the desk where the Finding of Cause lies with its one line empty.

options.label: Header and "previously"
options.consequence: The header, then two or three plain OOC lines: what happened last, what is owed, what is ticking that your PC knows of. Then the prose.
options.sample:
*Aetherion Academy, the old dispensary. The fifth day of term. First bell.*

((Previously: Harrowgate's Finding of Cause lies unsigned and is due now. Joan Aldery's letter went out under Rovhen's bare thumb. Sallow's cased plate from row six still sits on the Visitation desk.))

The bell is still counting over the east range when the Visitation runner reaches the dispensary door, one hand out, palm up.

options.label: The room recaps
options.consequence: No header; the first paragraph carries the recap through things in the room, the way R70-16's document opening does.
options.sample: First bell is counting over the east range. On the dispensary desk the Finding of Cause lies where it lay last night, the line beside *Party answerable* still bare, the ink dot dried to a black lentil. Beside it the leather is clean of dust in the shape of a folded letter, gone now to Joan Aldery under a bare thumb. Under the floor the hum has come back up with the morning draw, and at the door the Visitation runner holds out his hand.

questions.rec_reason: Three plain lines cost almost nothing and stop the drift the table data shows; the prose then opens clean, on the world, as a turn should.

questions.title: Who carries the Rumor Mill
questions.question: Which voices may carry the Rumor Mill's world news?
questions.context: NATALIE.md: two or three items "in an NPC's mouth, some wrong, one a hook." It has run once in the archive, Agnes Tull at the lodge. The Accord reads (R53-12); the Kharven hardly do. Every sample carries the east range cut for arrears (wrong), Sallow struck off for bribes (wrong), and a coroner's clerk asking after Mrs Aldery (true, the hook).

options.label: A gossip's mouth
options.consequence: One NPC who wants to know things first tells it and gets some of it wrong. NATALIE.md's form, and the teller becomes a standing face.
options.sample: Agnes Tull has the lodge door open before Rovhen reaches it, the keys already in her fist. "Board's cutting the east range, Instructor. Arrears. Your dispensary with it, so mind your lamps." The gap in her teeth whistles on the s. "And Master Sallow was struck off at Stannvaard for taking money off a factor, whatever he tells you. And a Mister Fenwick from the Deputy Coroner's came asking had we a Mrs Aldery lodging. I said we hadn't. We haven't."

options.label: Print and notice
options.consequence: Where the Inventory gives literacy, news arrives as a Board notice, a broadsheet or a porter's slate, and print can be wrong too. Never in the north.
options.sample: The lodge board carries three new things since last bell. A Board notice under green wax lists the east range for arrears, *plate to be cut within one turn*. A broadsheet pinned by one corner gives its third column to a ward-mender struck off the Stannvaard circuit *for consideration received*. And on the porters' slate, in chalk, in Agnes Tull's round hand: *Mr Fenwick, Dep. Coroner's office, called at the seventh hour for Mrs Aldery. Told not lodging.*

options.label: Overheard
options.consequence: Your PC passes people talking among themselves and catches the news in pieces, mixed in with their own business.
options.sample: On the east-range stair the Pryor brothers are carrying coal between them, one lamp for the two, and neither lowers his voice. "Board's cutting the range for arrears, Dunstan." "Board's always cutting something." "Sallow took money at Stannvaard. That's why they struck him." "Took it, or wouldn't?" "And there was a coroner's man at the lodge after the clerk-widow. Aldery." Hob shifts the scuttle to his other hip. "Mind the step. It's the bad one."

questions.rec_reason: Each culture gets the channel it really has, the wrong items always come from somewhere believable, and the teller's own want colours what you hear.

questions.title: When the Rumor Mill runs
questions.question: When does the Rumor Mill run?
questions.context: NATALIE.md runs it once, at session start. Sessions and story days rarely line up: one session can hold a week of downtime or ten minutes of a fight. Its wrong items are part of R48-42's frequent lies.

options.label: Session start
options.consequence: Two or three items as each session opens, as now.

options.label: Each new day
options.consequence: Two or three items with each new in-world day, however many days fall inside one session.

options.label: Each new place
options.consequence: On first arrival at a town, hall, camp or market, that place's own talk.

options.label: Only with a hook
options.consequence: It runs only when one item can carry a hook tied to a Front or the Ledger, and is skipped otherwise.

questions.rec_reason: The session opener keeps the habit alive and a new place's talk is where a traveller hears the world; daily rumours would flood a downtime week.

questions.title: The Scene Menu
questions.question: When you arrive without a beat, how are the three hooks offered?
questions.context: NATALIE.md: three hooks, one from a Front, one from the Ledger, one fresh; R70-97 adds a stated reward and penalty. No Scene Menu appears anywhere in the archive, since you nearly always bring a beat (your short prompt). A menu comes before the turn, so Table Rule 1's ban on OOC questions does not reach it. Every sample offers the same three hooks.

options.label: OOC list, then in-world
options.consequence: Three OOC lines, each with its source, reward and penalty; you pick in a word, and the turn opens on that hook in the world.
options.sample: ((Three ways in. Front: Imogen Pell wants the ring for the class by the sixth day. Reward, Class S owes Rovhen; penalty, she goes to the Visitation without him. Ledger: Sallow's bill for row six names Rovhen as witness. Reward, his word on the punch; penalty, the bursar enters Rovhen in the arrears. Fresh: Hobb and Mercer close for stocktake tonight. Reward, the back stair before it is scrubbed; penalty, Fenwick hears he was there.))

options.label: In-world notices
options.consequence: No list; the hooks arrive as the thread's own notices (a contract board where people read, a runner or a word at the fire where they do not), terms stated in the world.
options.sample: The lodge board has three new postings since last bell. In a tall, pressed hand: *The class wants the ring by the sixth day. Stand for us and Class S stands with you. Refuse, and we go to the Visitation. I.P.* In blunt capitals: *WITNESS WANTED TO A QUARTER PUNCH, ROW SIX. PAID AT THE GUILD HOUR. T. SALLOW.* And a draper's trade card, Hobb and Mercer, Tallow Street, *closed for stocktake tonight*, its back blank but for a pencilled hour.

options.label: Retire the menu
options.consequence: No menu at all; when you bring no beat, the most pressing Front moves and the turn opens on it.
options.sample: Imogen Pell is on the dispensary step before first bell, her slate under her arm and two Class S boys behind her, both a head taller and both looking at the door. She does not wait to be asked. "The class wants the ring, Instructor. Sixth day. We'd like you standing there when the Visitation says no." Behind her one of the boys shifts his weight. The slate stays shut against her ribs, her thumb along its edge.

questions.rec_reason: You choose in one word and the turn still opens in the world; R70-97's reward and penalty sit where you can weigh them, and the scene_menu tool already builds two of the three hooks.

questions.title: A turn sent back
questions.question: When you send a turn back to be redone, what goes with it?
questions.context: AI roleplay tools call a regenerated reply a swipe. Nothing in WOTR law covers it, though a discarded turn may already have logged a Ledger line, ticked a Front or set an NPC's voice. R49-01 lets you overrule a thought and R52-12 a voice; neither reaches a whole turn.

options.label: Unwound whole
options.consequence: A sent-back turn never happened: the prose is replaced and every table write it made (Ledger line, Front tick, roster entry) is reversed. Name any part to keep it.

options.label: Prose only
options.consequence: The writing is redone; the events and table writes stand unless you name one to go.

options.label: Natalie asks
options.consequence: Natalie asks in one OOC line which parts go, and redoes only those.

questions.rec_reason: It is what a send-back means, and it keeps the Ledger free of ghosts from a turn that never happened; one line from you saves anything worth keeping.

questions.title: Tense on Discord
questions.question: Does R49-02's present tense reach the posts Natalie writes for you on Discord?
questions.context: R49-02 puts roleplay turns "and work improved for a roleplay" in present tense. Every Discord post archived since it landed on 2026-09-26 is in past tense, either the server's habit or the rule not reaching it. Every sample renders one posted beat: Rovhen leaves the Finding unsigned and walks to the arena gate.

options.label: Present, as R49-02
options.consequence: Discord posts move to present tense like every roleplay turn; the past-tense posts already archived stay as filed.
options.sample: Rovhen leaves the Finding where it lies, its line still bare, and goes down past the runner on the stair. At the arena's north gate the chain holds the gate a hand's width open. The two sweepers lean on their brooms and watch him come, and the older one spits to the side, politely, away from him. Through the gap the trench runs straight across the sand, its walls sheared clean, and the air smells of scorched stone and wet ash.

options.label: The thread's own tense
options.consequence: This reopens R49-02: a Discord post follows the tense its thread already runs in, so it sits easily beside the other players' posts; Desktop turns stay present.
options.sample: Rovhen left the Finding where it lay, its line still bare, and went down past the runner on the stair. At the arena's north gate the chain held the gate a hand's width open. The two sweepers leaned on their brooms and watched him come, and the older one spat to the side, politely, away from him. Through the gap the trench ran straight across the sand, its walls sheared clean, and the air smelled of scorched stone and wet ash.

questions.rec_reason: Your own words on R49-02 named this exact case, making something "better for a roleplay", and one tense across both tables keeps the archive consistent.

questions.title: Your beat, expanded
questions.question: When Natalie turns your beat into a Discord post, what may she add?
questions.context: Natalie writes your characters' posts from your beat, and the house turns a few lines into 1,300 to 1,900 words. The 2026-09-21 ruling lets her improve your dialogue on an RP post; R52-09 lets her draft a missing line, marked, in written scenes. Other players' characters are never written (R71-6).

options.label: Researched mechanics
options.consequence: The real physics and anatomy under what he does (the grip escape toward the thumbs, the pressure wave of a strike), shown in the action, never lectured.

options.label: The room and walk-ons
options.consequence: Texture, the walk-on NPCs Natalie owns, and the room's reaction: the warden, the odds-maker, the porters.

options.label: Interior past the beat
options.consequence: His memory, feeling and reasoning beyond what you posted, under R49-01, which you may overrule line by line.

options.label: Lines you didn't post
options.consequence: New speech for him where your beat had none, marked as a draft for you to keep, change or cut before posting, as R52-09 does.

questions.rec_reason: These are what make the posts land and you have kept them every time; new speech in a public post is the one addition that should start in your own words.

settled.point: A roleplay turn runs about 3,500 words, filled half with texture and talk and half with the world moving; set pieces run 5,000 and up.
settled.why_not_asked: Your own answer ("3500"), ruled 2026-09-26. K3 asks only whether an OOC reply counts, and marks the two options that would reopen R49-30.

settled.point: NATALIE.md's Table Rule 2 bands (300 to 700, 700 to 1,500), its line "Over-delivery is the standing complaint" and the wotr-rp skill's "shorter turns" contradict R48-28 and R49-30.
settled.why_not_asked: A sweep owed, not a question; whatever K3 decides replaces them.

settled.point: Present tense for roleplay turns and work improved for a roleplay, past for written scenes and books; third person only.
settled.why_not_asked: Ruled 2026-09-26 and 2026-10-03. TU13 asks only whether it reaches the Discord posts, where practice has drifted.

settled.point: Narration may go to full depth inside your PC and you overrule any thought; your play beats the card; your characters stay yours in crossovers; the other creators' characters are never written.
settled.why_not_asked: Settled law. K6 asks only about involuntary reactions and what he would know outside a fight; TU14 only what a Discord post may add.

settled.point: Fights at the table: standing orders honoured, a player's fighter written as world facts with the read left to the player, and a findable way out always planted.
settled.why_not_asked: Ruled 2026-10-04 in the Combat Law. K5 asks only whether standing orders reach other scenes, K6 whether the world-fact rule does.

settled.point: A turn stops at your next decision and may stop mid-crisis, never on a summary or a question; quiet scenes may run kishōtenketsu (the four-part shape with no conflict) and still stop at your decision.
settled.why_not_asked: Ruled. TU2 asks only how far a talk turn runs before its stop.

settled.point: Natalie invents NPCs, places and texture without asking, logged; dull stretches pass in a line; big surprises need foreshadowing; nothing is rigged; death comes only if earned.
settled.why_not_asked: Ruled 2026-09-26. K2 asks only what "bigger things wait" should mean.

settled.point: You may take over any NPC's voice, and your version sticks.
settled.why_not_asked: Ruled; TU12 borrows it only to frame a sent-back turn.

settled.point: One italic thought per NPC in a roleplay turn; none under a POV lock in a written scene.
settled.why_not_asked: Ruled. The Cabin's two or three a turn is a lapse to fix, not a question.

settled.point: One crafted speech at a big moment outside court; long formal speech is the court register, the Accord chancery included.
settled.why_not_asked: Ruled 2026-09-26 and 2026-10-03. TU3 and TU4 ask only how several voices and routine talk share a turn.

settled.point: A full check on every turn; full notes in the scene file and a short summary in chat; one-line pushback, then keep writing; physics explained only when asked; research cited.
settled.why_not_asked: Ruled. TU6 and TU7 ask only where the summary sits at the Desktop table and what it carries.

settled.point: Every hook states a reward and a penalty, and quests are posted Guild and Crown contracts.
settled.why_not_asked: Ruled 2026-10-03. TU11 asks only how the Scene Menu offers its hooks.

settled.point: A turn may close on a short, clearly marked cut to what the POV cannot see.
settled.why_not_asked: Ruled. K7 asks only how often a cutaway runs and how much it shows.

settled.point: Opening modes (far to near, a season word, a document) and closing modes (mid-crisis, a notice or readout, breaking off before the payoff).
settled.why_not_asked: Ruled 2026-10-03. TU8 asks only what re-grounds a session's first turn.

settled.point: Numbers move only for a shown cause; an unsourced figure prints as a marked estimate; no number is invented.
settled.why_not_asked: Ruled. K2 relies on it so that numbers never wait for you.

settled.point: Each live thread keeps at least one openly warm bond.
settled.why_not_asked: Ruled 2026-10-03. K1's option D asks only whether every session owes it a moment.

settled.point: A new walk-on is a role until they speak twice or matter, then gets a name.
settled.why_not_asked: Ruled; it governs the walk-ons in TU3, TU9 and TU14 as written.

settled.point: Your dialogue is set verbatim in scene work and improved, meaning kept, when you ask for an RP post to be made better.
settled.why_not_asked: Ruled 2026-09-21. TU5 asks only whether the world may cut in, TU14 what else a post may add.

settled.point: One law governs every job, roleplay turns included.
settled.why_not_asked: Ruled 2026-10-03; every sample here is written under it.
